title: Sharks: Misunderstood Hunters
summary: Why sharks are fish to respect rather than monsters to fear: their many kinds, teeth, senses, rare bites, and important role in a healthy ocean.
poll: Sharks are more dangerous to people than people are to sharks.

versions.title: Sharks Are Not Bad
versions.text:
A fin cuts through the sea. It is a shark! Do you feel scared? Lots of kids do. But sharks are not mean.

Sharks are fish. There are more than five hundred kinds. Some are as small as your hand. The whale shark is the biggest fish of all. It is as long as a bus. But it eats tiny bits of food.

A shark is a predator. It hunts other sea life for food. The fish it eats are its prey.

Sharks have rows and rows of teeth. When a tooth falls out, a new one moves up. A shark can lose lots of teeth in its life.

Sharks have a great sense of smell. They can smell a drop of blood from far off. They can feel fish move in the water, too.

Sharks do not hunt people. Shark bites are rare. Most sharks swim away from us.

People are a big risk to sharks. We catch huge numbers each year. Sharks help keep the sea in good shape. We need to keep them safe.

versions.title: Sharks: Misunderstood Hunters
versions.text:
A gray fin slices through the waves, and swimmers rush toward the beach. Many people fear sharks more than almost any other animal, largely because frightening movies and exaggerated stories have given them a terrible reputation. However, much of what people believe about sharks is inaccurate, because sharks are not monsters but fish that hunt in order to survive, as countless other ocean creatures do.

Sharks are also extremely ancient, since their ancestors were swimming in the oceans more than four hundred million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs appeared. Today, scientists have identified more than five hundred species, which vary enormously in size. Some are smaller than a person's hand, while the whale shark is the largest fish on Earth and can grow longer than a school bus. Surprisingly, this gentle giant feeds on plankton, the tiny plants and animals that drift through the water, and whale sharks even visit the Red Sea along Saudi Arabia's western coast.

Unlike most fish, sharks have no bones. Instead, their skeleton is made of cartilage, the same flexible material that shapes your nose and ears, which keeps their bodies light and easy to bend.

A shark's mouth contains several rows of sharp teeth, and whenever a tooth breaks or falls out, another moves forward to replace it, so certain sharks lose thousands of teeth during their lives.

Sharks also possess remarkable senses. They can detect a tiny amount of blood from a considerable distance, special organs along their sides allow them to sense vibrations made by fish swimming nearby, and small pores on their snouts can even detect the weak electrical signals produced by living animals.

Sharks do not hunt people, and shark bites are extremely rare. In fact, humans are a far greater threat to sharks, since fishing fleets catch millions of them every year, often only for their valuable fins. Because most sharks grow slowly and have few young, their numbers recover slowly, which leaves many species vulnerable.

As apex predators at the top of the food chain, sharks help maintain the balance of the ocean ecosystem. They frequently catch sick or weak fish, which keeps fish populations healthy, so protecting sharks benefits the entire ocean.

Sharks are a greater danger to people.
People are a far greater threat to sharks.
The article does not compare them.
